answer.label: Earlier documented use by
answer.sourceLine: Trotsky records a shorter version in Literature and Revolution, chapter 4, in an English translation credited to Rose Strunsky (1925). He introduces it as something already said; the popular expanded wording has not been authenticated to Brecht.

source.excerpt: Art, it is said, is not a mirror, but a hammer: it does not reflect, it shapes.

author.name: Leon Trotsky
author.heading: About Leon Trotsky
author.bio: Leon Trotsky was a Russian revolutionary and a leading figure in the early Soviet state before his expulsion and exile. His Literature and Revolution examines competing artistic movements and the relationship between cultural production and social change.

cite.sourceCitation: Trotsky, Leon. Literature and Revolution. Chapter 4, “Futurism.” English translation credited to Rose Strunsky, 1925, as transcribed by the Marxists Internet Archive. Exact expanded headline wording untraced.
cite.pageCitation: Quotle.info. “Who really said ‘Art is not a mirror held up to society, but a hammer with which to shape it’?” Last verified 9 Nov 2026.

copyAttribution: Popular expanded variant of a saying recorded by Leon Trotsky in Literature and Revolution (English translation 1925); Trotsky says “it is said.” Original author and Brecht attribution unconfirmed.

misattribution.heading: An earlier record is not proof of coinage
misattribution.intro: The familiar Brecht credit lacks an authenticated original source.

items.why: Wikiquote ↗ marks the credit disputed and records the earlier Trotsky passage.

misattribution.truthLine: Describe Trotsky as an earlier recorder of an existing saying, not its established inventor.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Trotsky is discussing whether art can be reduced to a practical tool for changing society. After invoking the hammer image as a familiar claim, he adds that even learning to handle a hammer can involve a mirror, resisting the simple opposition.

That surrounding argument matters: quoting the metaphor alone can turn a qualified discussion into a slogan. Neither the primary passage nor its existence establishes that Trotsky coined the saying, and a later Brecht credit requires evidence of its own.
